options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to S3, create CloudWatch metrics from the logs using metric filters, set up CloudWatch anomaly detection on invocation count, latency, and error rate metrics, and configure composite alarms with SNS notifications.
Use AWS CloudTrail to log all Bedrock API calls and create an Athena query that runs hourly to check for errors in the CloudTrail logs.
Implement application-level logging using console.log statements that write to CloudWatch Logs, and have the on-call engineer review logs daily.
Use AWS X-Ray to trace all Bedrock API calls and set up X-Ray insights to send email notifications when latency exceeds a static threshold.

explanation: Enabling Bedrock model invocation logging provides detailed metrics on every invocation. CloudWatch anomaly detection uses machine learning to establish dynamic baselines and detect unusual patterns, which is more effective than static thresholds for AI workloads with variable traffic. Composite alarms correlate multiple signals (error rate + latency + volume) to reduce false positives. SNS notifications provide proactive alerting. CloudTrail (B) captures API control plane events but not invocation-level performance metrics, and hourly Athena queries are not real-time. Console.log with daily review (C) is entirely reactive and will miss issues for hours. X-Ray (D) is useful for distributed tracing but relies on static thresholds, which produce excessive false alarms for AI workloads with naturally variable latency.

domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
stem: A company is optimizing the latency of its Amazon Bedrock-powered real-time recommendation engine. The current architecture sends a 4,000-token system prompt with every API request, and the average end-to-end response time is 3.5 seconds. The application serves globally distributed users, with 60% of traffic originating from Asia-Pacific. Which TWO optimizations would MOST effectively reduce latency? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to cache the static 4,000-token system prompt, reducing time-to-first-token for subsequent requests that reuse the same prompt prefix.
Compress the system prompt using gzip encoding before sending it to the Bedrock API to reduce network transfer time.

Deploy the application in an Asia-Pacific Region where Bedrock is available and use the Bedrock endpoint in that Region for Asia-Pacific users, reducing network round-trip time for the majority of traffic.
Increase the max_tokens parameter to allow the model to generate longer responses, which triggers faster processing in the model.

explanation: Bedrock prompt caching (A) avoids reprocessing the same 4,000-token system prompt on every request. Since the system prompt is static and repeated, caching it significantly reduces time-to-first-token and overall latency. Deploying in an Asia-Pacific Region (C) reduces network latency for 60% of users by placing the inference endpoint closer to them, reducing round-trip time. Gzip compression (B) is not supported by the Bedrock API — the API accepts JSON payloads, not compressed binary, and tokens are processed by the model regardless of wire format. Increasing max_tokens (D) does not speed up processing; it only raises the upper bound on output length and could actually increase latency if the model generates more tokens.

stem: A machine learning team has deployed a text summarization model on Amazon Bedrock and needs to evaluate summary quality programmatically before promoting the model to production. The summaries must preserve factual content from the source documents, and the team wants a metric that measures n-gram overlap between the generated summary and reference summaries. They also need to run evaluations at scale without managing infrastructure. Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock model evaluation with a BLEU score metric on a curated evaluation dataset, and set a minimum threshold score as a promotion gate.
Use Amazon Bedrock model evaluation with a ROUGE score metric on a curated evaluation dataset, and set a minimum threshold score as a promotion gate.
Deploy a custom BERTScore evaluation pipeline on Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs and store results in Amazon S3 for manual review before promotion.
Implement human evaluation using Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth labeling workflows and require a majority vote from three annotators before promotion.

explanation: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is the standard metric for evaluating text summarization quality by measuring n-gram overlap between generated and reference summaries. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation supports ROUGE as a built-in metric, allowing the team to run evaluations at scale without managing infrastructure. BLEU (Option A) is primarily designed for machine translation evaluation, not summarization. BERTScore (Option C) measures semantic similarity using embeddings rather than n-gram overlap, and deploying a custom pipeline on SageMaker adds unnecessary infrastructure management. Human evaluation (Option D) does not measure n-gram overlap and is not programmatic.

stem: A company uses a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline built with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Users report that the chatbot frequently provides answers that are factually correct but irrelevant to the user's actual question. The development team confirms that the foundation model performs well when given the correct context. What is the MOST likely root cause and the appropriate fix?

options.text: The foundation model is hallucinating due to a high temperature setting. Lower the temperature parameter to 0.1 to produce more deterministic outputs.
The embedding model is producing low-quality vector representations. Replace the embedding model with Amazon Titan Embeddings V2 for improved semantic encoding.

The chunking strategy is creating chunks that are too large, causing the retriever to return broadly relevant but imprecise passages. Reduce the chunk size and increase chunk overlap to improve retrieval precision.
The knowledge base index is stale and contains outdated documents. Trigger a re-sync of the data source to refresh the vector index with current content.

explanation: When a RAG pipeline returns answers that are factually correct but irrelevant to the specific question, the issue lies in retrieval precision. Overly large chunks cause the retriever to match on broadly related content rather than the precise passage needed. Reducing chunk size and increasing overlap ensures that retrieved passages are more narrowly focused on the query's intent. Option A is incorrect because the model performs well with correct context, so hallucination is not the issue. Option B is unlikely since the embeddings are producing relevant (though imprecise) matches. Option D would cause outdated answers, not irrelevant ones to current questions.

stem: A fintech startup runs a customer-facing generative AI assistant on Amazon Bedrock. After a recent prompt template update, users report that the assistant occasionally fabricates regulatory compliance details that do not exist. The team needs to detect and reduce these hallucinations systematically. Which combination of actions should the team take FIRST?

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with a denied topics filter for regulatory content and add a grounding check that validates responses against a curated knowledge base of actual regulations.
Switch to a larger foundation model with more parameters to improve factual accuracy, and increase the max token limit to allow the model to generate more comprehensive responses.
Add a disclaimer to all responses stating that regulatory information may be inaccurate, and implement a feedback button so users can flag hallucinated content for manual review.
Fine-tune the foundation model on a dataset of verified regulatory documents using Amazon Bedrock custom model training to encode factual compliance knowledge into the model weights.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides built-in hallucination mitigation through grounding checks that validate model responses against authoritative source documents. Combining a grounding check with denied topics filtering provides a systematic, immediate defense against fabricated regulatory content. Option B is incorrect because a larger model does not inherently prevent hallucinations and may increase them. Option C does not actually prevent hallucinations, only acknowledges them. Option D is a longer-term effort and fine-tuning alone does not guarantee elimination of hallucinations, making it unsuitable as a first response.

stem: A data science team is deploying a real-time inference endpoint on Amazon SageMaker for a custom language model. During load testing, they observe that the first few requests after deployment take 15-20 seconds to respond, while subsequent requests complete in under 2 seconds. The team needs to ensure consistently low latency for all requests. What should they do?

options.text: Increase the instance type to a larger GPU instance with more memory to speed up model loading during cold starts.
Enable SageMaker inference recommender to automatically select the optimal instance type and container configuration for the workload.
Configure the endpoint with a minimum instance count greater than zero and enable model data download ahead of time by using SageMaker's keep-warm behavior or provisioned concurrency.
Implement client-side retry logic with exponential backoff to handle cold start timeouts, and increase the endpoint timeout from 60 to 120 seconds.

explanation: The 15-20 second delay on initial requests is a classic cold start problem where the model must be loaded into memory before inference can begin. Setting a minimum instance count greater than zero ensures that at least one instance is always warm and ready to serve requests. SageMaker's keep-warm behavior prevents instances from being scaled down to zero. Option A does not solve cold starts because even larger instances need time to load the model initially. Option B helps select the right instance but does not prevent cold starts. Option D masks the problem with retries rather than fixing the root cause of high initial latency.

stem: A healthcare company uses Amazon Bedrock to power a medical information assistant. The compliance team requires continuous monitoring of the AI system's behavior in production. They need to detect model quality degradation, track prompt-response patterns for audit purposes, and receive alerts when output quality drops below acceptable thresholds. Which THREE actions should the team implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to capture all prompts, responses, and metadata in Amazon S3 and CloudWatch Logs for audit trail and analysis.
Deploy Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor with a custom monitoring schedule to detect data drift and model quality degradation on the Bedrock endpoint.

Create CloudWatch custom metrics from the invocation logs to track response quality indicators such as response length, latency percentiles, and error rates, with CloudWatch Alarms for threshold breaches.
Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with content filters and topic restrictions, and enable CloudWatch metrics for guardrail intervention rates to monitor output quality boundaries.
Implement AWS X-Ray distributed tracing on the Bedrock API calls to automatically score response quality and trigger SNS notifications for low-quality outputs.

explanation: Option A enables comprehensive logging of all model interactions for audit compliance, capturing prompts, completions, and metadata. Option C creates actionable monitoring by converting logs into custom CloudWatch metrics with alarms for quality degradation. Option D provides real-time output quality guardrails and monitors intervention rates as a proxy for quality issues. Option B is incorrect because SageMaker Model Monitor is designed for SageMaker endpoints, not Amazon Bedrock endpoints. Option E is incorrect because AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing for latency analysis but does not automatically score response quality.

stem: An e-commerce company wants to compare two different foundation models for their product description generator before committing to one. They need to measure which model produces descriptions that lead to higher user engagement while ensuring statistical significance. The system currently serves 50,000 requests per day. Which approach provides the MOST reliable comparison?

options.text: Run both models offline on the same 1,000 product inputs, have domain experts score the outputs on a 1-5 scale, and select the model with the higher average score.

Deploy both models behind an Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda function that randomly routes 50% of traffic to each model, log user engagement metrics to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, and use statistical hypothesis testing to compare conversion rates after sufficient sample size is reached.
Run Amazon Bedrock model evaluation using built-in automatic metrics on a benchmark dataset, and select the model with the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores as the production model.
Deploy Model A for one week, then deploy Model B for the following week, compare aggregate engagement metrics from CloudWatch dashboards, and select the model with better weekly performance.

explanation: A proper A/B test with random traffic splitting is the most reliable way to measure real user engagement differences between models. Routing 50% of traffic to each model simultaneously eliminates temporal confounding variables (seasonality, marketing campaigns), and statistical hypothesis testing ensures the results are significant. Option A uses expert evaluation, which measures perceived quality but not actual user engagement. Option C uses automatic metrics that do not capture user engagement (clicks, conversions). Option D uses a sequential test that introduces time-based confounders, making it impossible to attribute differences solely to the model.

stem: A development team maintains a generative AI application that uses Amazon Bedrock with a carefully engineered system prompt. They are preparing to update the system prompt to improve response formatting. Before deploying the change, they need to ensure the new prompt does not cause regressions in answer quality across their existing test scenarios. Which testing strategy is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Deploy the new prompt to a staging environment and have QA engineers manually test 20 representative queries to verify acceptable output quality before promoting to production.

Create an automated prompt regression test suite that runs the new prompt against a curated dataset of input-expected output pairs, uses an LLM-as-a-judge to score each response against acceptance criteria, and fails the deployment pipeline if scores fall below established baselines.
Use Amazon Bedrock's built-in prompt versioning to maintain both prompts simultaneously, and gradually shift traffic from the old prompt to the new one using weighted routing over 48 hours.
Run the new prompt through Amazon Bedrock model evaluation with automatic metrics, compare ROUGE scores against the old prompt's evaluation results, and deploy if scores are equal or higher.

explanation: An automated prompt regression test suite integrated into the CI/CD pipeline provides systematic, repeatable verification that prompt changes do not degrade quality. Using an LLM-as-a-judge approach enables nuanced evaluation of free-form text outputs against specific acceptance criteria at scale. This catches regressions before deployment. Option A is insufficient because manual testing of only 20 queries is not comprehensive and does not scale. Option C deploys the untested prompt to production, risking user-facing regressions. Option D relies on ROUGE scores, which measure n-gram overlap but may not capture the formatting and quality dimensions the team cares about.

stem: A media company's generative AI application invokes Amazon Bedrock's Claude model through an API. During peak hours, the application experiences intermittent ThrottlingException errors, causing some user requests to fail. CloudWatch metrics show that the provisioned throughput is being exceeded. The team needs to resolve this issue while maintaining the best possible user experience. What should they do?

options.text: Implement exponential backoff with jitter in the application's retry logic, increase the Bedrock provisioned throughput quota, and add an Amazon SQS queue to buffer requests during peak periods.
Switch from on-demand to batch inference using Amazon Bedrock batch jobs to process all requests asynchronously, and notify users when their responses are ready.
Deploy a caching layer using Amazon ElastiCache to store previous model responses and serve identical queries from cache, eliminating the need for additional Bedrock throughput.
Distribute requests across multiple AWS Regions by deploying the application in three Regions with Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to spread the load across regional Bedrock endpoints.

explanation: The correct approach combines three complementary strategies: exponential backoff with jitter handles transient throttling gracefully, increasing provisioned throughput addresses the capacity shortfall, and an SQS queue buffers excess requests during peak periods to smooth out traffic spikes. Option B degrades user experience by making all requests asynchronous, which is inappropriate for an interactive application. Option C only helps for repeated identical queries, which is rare in generative AI applications where inputs vary. Option D adds complexity and cost, and model availability and quotas vary by Region, so it does not guarantee resolution.

stem: A company has deployed a custom text generation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. After three months in production, they notice that the model's output quality has gradually declined, and user satisfaction scores have dropped by 20%. The training data was representative of user queries at launch time. Which TWO factors are the MOST likely causes of this degradation, and what monitoring should be implemented to detect such issues earlier?

options.text: Data drift: the distribution of user inputs has shifted over time compared to the training data. Implement SageMaker Model Monitor with a data quality monitoring schedule to detect statistical deviations in input feature distributions.

GPU memory fragmentation on the SageMaker endpoint instances caused by continuous inference requests. Implement CloudWatch metrics for GPU memory utilization and set auto-scaling policies to rotate instances weekly.

Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and expected outputs has changed due to evolving user expectations or domain changes. Implement SageMaker Model Monitor with a model quality monitoring schedule that tracks prediction accuracy against ground truth labels.
The SageMaker endpoint's auto-scaling policy reduced the instance count during off-peak hours, causing request queuing and degraded response quality due to increased latency.

The model artifact stored in Amazon S3 has been corrupted over time due to bit rot in the S3 object storage. Implement S3 data integrity checks and redeploy the model from the original training artifact.

explanation: Gradual quality degradation over months is a hallmark of data drift and concept drift. Data drift (Option A) occurs when the input distribution changes over time, meaning the model encounters queries it was not trained to handle well. SageMaker Model Monitor's data quality monitoring detects this by comparing incoming data distributions against a baseline. Concept drift (Option C) occurs when the meaning of what constitutes a good output changes, even if the inputs are similar. Model quality monitoring tracks metrics against ground truth to detect this. Option B is incorrect because GPU memory fragmentation does not cause gradual quality decline. Option D describes a latency issue, not output quality degradation. Option E is incorrect because S3 provides 99.999999999% durability and does not suffer from bit rot.

stem: A developer is troubleshooting a RAG application that uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Users report that the application sometimes returns "I don't know" even for questions that are clearly covered in the ingested documents. CloudWatch Logs show that the retrieval step returns zero results for these queries. The developer confirms that the documents are properly ingested and the vector index contains the expected embeddings. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The OpenSearch Serverless collection has reached its storage capacity limit, causing new queries to be rejected by the vector search engine.
The similarity score threshold in the knowledge base retrieval configuration is set too high, filtering out relevant results that fall below the threshold despite being semantically related.
The Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base is configured with the wrong foundation model for answer generation, causing it to refuse to answer even when context is retrieved.
The IAM execution role for the Bedrock Knowledge Base lacks s3:GetObject permissions on the source document bucket, preventing retrieval of document content at query time.

explanation: When the retrieval step returns zero results despite confirmed ingestion and valid embeddings, the most likely cause is an overly restrictive similarity score threshold. The knowledge base filters out results whose similarity score falls below the configured threshold. If this threshold is set too high, semantically related but not exactly matching results are discarded, leading to empty retrieval. Option A is incorrect because storage capacity issues would prevent ingestion, not retrieval. Option C is incorrect because the logs show zero retrieval results, meaning the issue is in retrieval, not generation. Option D is incorrect because the documents are already ingested; the IAM role for retrieval accesses the vector store, not the original S3 documents.

stem: A company is preparing to launch a generative AI-powered customer support chatbot built on Amazon Bedrock. Before going live, the team must perform comprehensive load testing to validate that the system can handle 500 concurrent users with a p99 latency target of 10 seconds. Which THREE practices should the team follow to conduct an effective load test for this AI workload?

options.text: Use realistic prompt distributions in the load test that mirror expected production traffic patterns, including varying prompt lengths, complexity levels, and topic categories, rather than using a single repeated test prompt.
Perform the load test during off-peak hours only to ensure consistent results, and extrapolate the performance to peak hours by applying a linear scaling factor to the measured latencies.

Monitor Amazon Bedrock service-level throttling metrics alongside application-level metrics during the test, and verify that the account's provisioned throughput and token-per-minute quotas are sufficient for the target concurrency.
Set the max token generation parameter to the minimum possible value during load testing to minimize costs, then increase it to the production value after validating concurrency targets.

Implement a gradual ramp-up pattern that increases concurrent users incrementally while measuring latency at each level to identify the concurrency threshold where p99 latency exceeds the 10-second target.

explanation: Effective load testing for generative AI requires: (A) Realistic prompt distributions because response latency varies significantly with prompt length and complexity, so using a single test prompt would produce misleading results. (C) Monitoring service-level quotas because Amazon Bedrock enforces tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute limits that directly impact achievable concurrency. (E) Gradual ramp-up to identify the exact concurrency threshold where latency targets are breached, enabling capacity planning. Option B is incorrect because linear extrapolation does not account for non-linear behavior under load, and Bedrock's shared infrastructure may behave differently at different times. Option D is incorrect because reducing max tokens fundamentally changes the workload characteristics, making the test results invalid for production capacity planning.
